review.review_summary: 9 claims checked against the evidence; 1 flagged (1 overstated).
gaps: The analysis does not examine whether support tickets relate to revenue *changes* (contraction or expansion MRR) rather than absolute MRR levels. A customer with high MRR who contracts may show a different ticket pattern than one with low MRR who expands.
No breakdown of support tickets by customer cohort or plan type is provided. The relationship between tickets and revenue may differ for new versus established customers, or across plan tiers.
The analysis does not explore temporal patterns: whether tickets in one month predict revenue changes in the following month, or whether ticket spikes coincide with contraction events.
next_investigations: Compute the correlation between support tickets and month-over-month MRR change (or contraction/expansion flags) for each customer, then average across the 200 customers. This tests whether tickets predict revenue *movement* rather than absolute level.
Segment customers by contraction status (those with negative MRR change in the 12-month window versus those without) and compare median support tickets between groups.
Lag support tickets by one month and correlate with MRR change in the following month to test whether ticket volume in month N predicts revenue movement in month N+1.
methodology_concerns: The correlation is computed across 6,000 snapshots (one row per account per billing date), not 200 independent customers. Repeated measures of the same customer over 30 months violate independence assumptions and may inflate or deflate the correlation estimate.

The evidence reports medium confidence for a weak association (|r| = 0.04). Medium confidence typically reflects adequate sample size but does not guarantee the association is meaningful in practice; the threshold for 'negligible' is not defined in the evidence.

claims.text: Support tickets and monthly recurring revenue show no meaningful relationship in this dataset.

Across 6,000 snapshots covering 200 customers, support tickets and monthly recurring revenue move together only negligibly, making it unlikely that ticket volume is a reliable signal of revenue health.
The more notable revenue story is that net revenue retention has declined and contraction MRR is the primary drag on growth.
The association between support tickets and monthly recurring revenue is negligible and could easily be chance — the two measures barely move together across all 6,000 rows.

Support tickets range from 0 to 11 with a median of 3, while monthly recurring revenue ranges from $35.44 to $1,023.37 with a median of $87.35 — the wide spread in revenue with no corresponding pattern in tickets reinforces that the two are unrelated.

Net revenue retention fell to 106.5% (12 months to 31 Oct 2026) from 122.7% a year earlier, driven by contraction MRR of $13,587.47 against expansion MRR of $16,056.28 — a dynamic that ticket volume does not appear to explain.
No customers churned in the window and logo churn held at 0.0%, so the revenue pressure is entirely from existing customers contracting, not leaving.

Investigate contraction MRR drivers directly — interview or survey the customers who contracted — rather than relying on support ticket volume as a proxy. Contraction MRR is the sole drag on net revenue retention and its cause is currently unexplained by the available data.

Enrich the dataset with ticket category, severity, or resolution time and re-run the analysis to test whether a specific ticket type relates to revenue changes. Raw ticket counts show no signal; a more granular ticket attribute might reveal a relationship that volume alone cannot.

Read as SaaS subscription data (MRR, ARR, paying customers, new MRR, churned MRR, logo churn, net revenue retention, gross revenue retention). MRR is the monthly run-rate of the customers paying at the latest date (an annual plan ÷ 12, net of discounts; trials, paused and unpaid subscriptions out, past due in), not revenue; movements and retention compare each customer's MRR at month-ends over the 12 months to that date, and annual churn is measured on the customers paying 12 months earlier, never a monthly rate × 12. A customer who starts and leaves inside one month appears in no month-end figure.
The churned column is a flag, not a dated event: the share of rows flagged is not a churn rate.
